title: Mexico Reduces Its Illiteracy Rate to 3.8%: Public Education Secretariat
author: Fernanda Monroy
content:
_This article by[Fernanda
Monroy](https://contralinea.com.mx/author/fermonroy/) originally appeared in
the [September 8, 2026 edition of
Contralínea](https://contralinea.com.mx/interno/semana/mexico-reduce-a-3-8-su-
tasa-de-analfabetismo-sep/), an independent Mexican investigative magazine._

Mexico reduced its illiteracy rate **from 4.1 to 3.8 percent** in the first
year of the National Literacy Strategy for Shared Well-being, reaching **the
lowest level recorded in the country’s history** , reported the Secretary of
Public Education, Mario Delgado Carrillo.

During the commemoration of the 60th Anniversary of International Literacy
Day, on September 8, the official highlighted that **more than 277,000 people
learned to read and write** over the past year. To this are added 323,000
people who completed primary school and nearly 542,000 who finished secondary
school.

The Public Education Secretary attributed these results to the strategy
launched in 2025 through the National Institute for Adult Education (INEA),
and maintained that teaching literacy represents an act of justice and equity.

“It is one of the deepest acts of justice, equity, and love that can be
carried out,” said the secretary, who linked the literacy policy to the Fourth
Transformation’s principle of placing the most vulnerable people at the center
of public policy.

> “It is one of the deepest acts of justice, equity, and love that can be
> carried out.”
>
> Mario Delgado Carrillo, Secretary of Public Education

He also noted that these advances are part of the goal of building an
“Educating Republic,” one of the 100 commitments established by President
Sheinbaum.

This effort involves the INEA and the State Institutes for Adult Education,
through Community Centers (Plazas Comunitarias) and Study Circles. Volunteers
and high school and university students have also been incorporated to support
both literacy and the continuation of studies.

The Public Education Secretary maintained that reducing illiteracy will
continue to be a priority, and assured that the federal government will not
stop working until this lag is diminished.

He recalled that, 45 years after its creation, the INEA has helped more than
**32.4 million Mexicans** over the age of 15 complete some level of education,
through free literacy, primary, and secondary school services.

The commemoration was held in Chiapas, where Governor Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar
highlighted the Chiapas Puede (Chiapas Can) program, aimed at reducing the
educational lag in the state’s communities.

The governor maintained that teaching literacy is a way to accompany and
transform people’s lives, so he called on families, students, teachers, and
young people to join the teaching efforts to extend the program to communities
that still face difficulties in accessing basic education. “To teach literacy
is to love,” he said, referring to the cases of people who have learned to
read and write through this strategy.

During the event, literacy teacher Luis López Díaz stressed the importance of
bringing these tools to communities where older adults and parents had not had
access to reading and writing.

He explained that, through the Chiapas Puede and Alfabetizar es Amar (Teaching
Literacy Is Loving) programs, some of these people can now identify letters
and understand official documents, including those related to their identity.

In turn, the Assistant Director-General of UNESCO, Lidia Arthur Brito,
recognized the work carried out by Mexico on literacy and noted that the
experiences implemented in the country constitute practices that can
contribute to the international exchange of strategies to address the
educational lag.
